keyTerms.definition: The actualization of a potential: something that was potentially F becomes actually F. Aristotelians distinguish four kinds — qualitative, local (change of place), quantitative, and substantial.
keyTerms.example: Hot coffee (potentially cold) becomes actually cold.

keyTerms.definition: The way a thing actually is, here and now; its realized features. Only what is actual can do anything or cause anything.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s actual heat; the actual coolness of the room’s air.

keyTerms.definition: A real but unrealized capacity of a thing to be or become some way. It is not nothing — it is a determinate range of what a thing can become, which excludes other possibilities.
keyTerms.example: Coffee can become cold or stain the carpet, but cannot become chicken soup or a live chicken.

keyTerms.definition: The ancient argument that change is impossible because it would require something (e.g. coldness) to come from nothing. Aristotle answers it by showing that what comes to be was already present potentially.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s coldness seems to spring from nothing — but it was there all along as a potential.

keyTerms.definition: Qualitative (a quality changes), local (place changes), quantitative (size or amount changes), substantial (one kind of substance becomes another).
keyTerms.example: Coffee cooling; a leaf falling; a puddle growing; a swatted fly dying.

keyTerms.definition: No potential can be actualized except by something already actual; whatever goes from potential to actual is caused. It follows from the nature of potentiality, not merely from observed regularities.
keyTerms.example: The coffee’s potential coldness can’t make itself actual; the air’s actual coolness must do it.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever actualizes a potential in something else. It need not itself be changing, but if it is, its own change needs an actualizer.
keyTerms.example: The air conditioner actualizes the air’s potential to be cool.

keyTerms.definition: A series of causes extended through time in which each member has its causal power on its own (relative to the others), so it can go on acting after earlier members are gone. Feser grants that such a series might have no first member.
keyTerms.example: Button → air conditioner → cool air → cold coffee; Al begets Bob, who begets Chuck.

keyTerms.definition: A series in which every member except the first has its causal power only derivatively, as an instrument, and acts only insofar as it is being acted on by an earlier member here and now. It must have a first member.
keyTerms.example: Earth holds up foundation, which holds up floor, which holds up desk, which holds up cup.

keyTerms.definition: A cause that has its causal power borrowed from another and exercises it only while that other acts through it.
keyTerms.example: The paintbrush in a painter’s hand; the stick moved by a hand to move a stone.

keyTerms.definition: A cause with underived, ‘built-in’ causal power — one that can actualize without itself being actualized. ‘First’ means first in rank or in the order of dependence, not earliest in time or ‘number one’ in a finite list.
keyTerms.example: The painter, relative to brush and paint; ultimately, the purely actual actualizer.

keyTerms.definition: That which has no potentiality at all — no capacity to be other than it is — and therefore needs no actualizer. It does not merely have actuality; it is actuality itself. (The traditional scholastic Latin is actus purus.)
keyTerms.example: The terminus of every hierarchical series of actualizers of existence.

keyTerms.definition: Feser’s more precise name for Aristotle’s Unmoved Mover: a cause that actualizes other things without being actualized. The chapter argues it must be unmovable (purely actual), not merely unmoved in fact.
keyTerms.example: What keeps the water (and everything else) in existence at every instant.

keyTerms.definition: A cause of a thing’s continuing existence here and now, as opposed to the cause that originally brought it about. The Aristotelian proof is ultimately about sustaining causes.
keyTerms.example: Not the brewing that made the coffee, but what makes its matter exist as coffee right now.

keyTerms.definition: Aristotle’s analysis of material substances as composites of substantial form (what makes it the kind of thing it is) and prime matter (the pure potential to take on form). Feser’s footnote shows the argument can be restated in these terms.
keyTerms.example: Water is not a heap of atoms but a substance whose atoms exist in it only ‘virtually’.

keyTerms.definition: The absence of a feature a thing’s nature requires for completeness — a failure to realize a potential proper to it. Imperfection and badness are privations.
keyTerms.example: A squirrel crippled by a car; a tree with damaged roots.

keyTerms.definition: The degree to which a thing has actualized the potentials proper to it and is free of privation. Pure actuality has maximal perfection.
keyTerms.example: A healthy, fully grown oak is more perfect as an oak than a stunted, diseased one.

keyTerms.definition: A thing is good to the extent it realizes the potentials inherent in its kind, bad to the extent it fails to. Pure actuality, lacking nothing, is fully good.
keyTerms.example: A good painter has actualized his potential for craftsmanship and composition.

keyTerms.definition: There can be only one purely actual being, because distinguishing two would require a differentiating feature — which would mean some potential or privation in one of them.
keyTerms.example: Two trees differ in size, location, sturdiness of roots; nothing like that can distinguish two pure acts.

keyTerms.definition: Whatever is in an effect must be in its cause in some way — formally, virtually, or eminently — since a cause cannot give what it doesn’t have.
keyTerms.example: I can give you $20 only if I have it somehow: in my wallet, in my bank account, or via the power to print it.

keyTerms.definition: Three ways a cause can ‘have’ what is in its effect: formally (it has the very same feature), virtually (it has the power to obtain or produce it), eminently (it has it in a higher way, e.g. the power to bring such things into existence in the first place).
keyTerms.example: Twenty in the wallet (formal); twenty in the bank (virtual); authority to print twenties (eminent).

keyTerms.definition: The capacity to grasp universal concepts, combine them into thoughts, and reason from thought to thought. Its essence is having the form of a thing without being that kind of thing.
keyTerms.example: You grasp triangularity without becoming a triangle.

keyTerms.definition: What makes a thing the kind of thing it is. It can exist concretely in individual things or abstractly in an intellect.
keyTerms.example: The form shared by all triangles, or by all men.

keyTerms.definition: The formal cause is a thing’s nature or form, which grounds how it behaves; the efficient cause is what produces or sustains it.
keyTerms.example: Lead-210’s nature grounds its probability of decay (formal); what generated it and keeps it in being are efficient causes.

keyTerms.definition: Physics’ method of describing only those aspects of nature that can be captured mathematically. This explains its precision but guarantees it omits qualitative and causal features.
keyTerms.example: A metal detector finds only metal; that doesn’t show there’s no wood.

keyTerms.definition: Minkowski’s four-dimensional interpretation of relativity, on which past, present and future are equally real, so change is (allegedly) illusory. Feser calls it a picture of actuality without potentiality.
keyTerms.example: Moments of time treated like places on a map, all equally ‘there’.

keyTerms.definition: The cause directly producing an effect, which is simultaneous with it as part of the same event (simultaneous need not mean instantaneous).
keyTerms.example: The brick pressing into the glass (not the earlier throw) is the immediate cause of the glass giving way.

keyTerms.definition: Treating a merely contingent feature of the cases one has observed as if it were essential to the kind.
keyTerms.example: Every U.S. president has been under seven feet tall, so no one seven feet tall could be president.

keyTerms.definition: Arbitrarily exempting one case from a rule applied to others. The ‘What caused God?’ objection accuses the argument of this; the charge fails because the exemption follows from the rule’s own rationale.
keyTerms.example: Things need causes because they have potentials; pure act has none, so it is no arbitrary exception.

distinctions.name: Per accidens vs. per se causal series

left.label: Per accidens (linear, accidentally ordered)
left.desc: Members are strung out in time and each has its own causal power relative to the others; a later member can keep acting after earlier ones disappear (the air conditioner runs after you leave; Bob begets Chuck whether or not Al is alive). Such a series could in principle have no beginning.

right.label: Per se (hierarchical, essentially ordered)
right.desc: Every member but the first has only derived, instrumental power and acts only while being acted on (desk held by floor held by foundation). Remove the source and the whole series stops at once. It must have a first member with underived power — even if it were infinitely long.

distinctions.whyItMatters: This is the hinge of the entire proof. The argument concedes an infinite past and rests everything on the per se series that sustains things in being right now. Most popular objections (‘the universe might be eternal’, ‘why can’t the chain go back forever?’) confuse the two.

distinctions.name: Actuality vs. potentiality

left.label: Actuality
left.desc: What a thing actually is here and now; only the actual can act or cause.

right.label: Potentiality
right.desc: What a thing can become — real but unrealized, determinate (coffee can cool, not turn into soup), and incapable of actualizing itself.

distinctions.whyItMatters: It explains change without Parmenides’ something-from-nothing, grounds the principle of causality, and defines the conclusion (pure actuality) from which every divine attribute is derived.

distinctions.name: ‘First’ in time vs. ‘first’ in the order of dependence

left.label: Temporally first
left.desc: The earliest member of a series, the one at the beginning — e.g., whatever triggered the Big Bang.

right.label: First as primary / underived
right.desc: The member whose causal power is built in rather than borrowed, and on which all the others depend right now for their power to act.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The argument’s First Cause is first in the second sense. That is why the age of the universe, and whether time had a beginning, are irrelevant.

distinctions.name: Cause of coming-to-be vs. cause of being (sustaining cause)

left.label: Cause of becoming
left.desc: What originally produced a thing — the brewing of the coffee, the chemical reaction that bonded hydrogen and oxygen, the parents who begot a child.

right.label: Cause of being
right.desc: What makes the thing exist right now, at this instant — what actualizes the matter’s potential to be water rather than separate gases here and now.

distinctions.whyItMatters: The argument asks the second question. Answers to the first (‘a past process made it’) or about possible destruction (‘nothing has broken it up yet’) don’t touch it.

distinctions.name: ‘Everything has a cause’ vs. ‘whatever goes from potential to actual has a cause’

left.label: The straw man
left.desc: Everything whatsoever has a cause — which would indeed make ‘What caused God?’ a fair question.

right.label: The actual principle
right.desc: Only what passes from potency to act needs an actualizer; what is purely actual has nothing to be actualized, so it neither needs nor could have a cause.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Keeping them apart defuses the most common objection to every first-cause argument. The difference is like that between ‘all triangles have three sides’ and ‘all figures have three sides’.

distinctions.name: Formal vs. virtual vs. eminent possession of an effect

left.label: Formally
left.desc: The cause has the very feature it gives (I hand you a twenty from my wallet).

right.label: Virtually or eminently
right.desc: The cause has the power to obtain it (bank credit) or the higher power to produce such things at all (authority to print money).

distinctions.whyItMatters: Proportionate causality does not mean God must be a cat to cause cats. The forms of things are in God eminently — as ideas in an intellect — which is how Stage 2 derives intelligence and omniscience.

distinctions.name: Absence from the representation vs. representation of absence

left.label: Absent from the representation
left.desc: A black-and-white drawing contains no color; mathematical physics contains no ‘causes’, only equations.

right.label: Represented as absent
right.desc: A claim that the scene itself is colorless, or that nature itself lacks causation.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Russell’s, Newtonian, relativistic and quantum objections all slide from the first to the second. If a method is guaranteed to leave something out, its omission is no evidence the thing is missing.

distinctions.name: Unmoved vs. unmovable

left.label: Unmoved (in fact)
left.desc: A first actualizer that isn’t actually being actualized while it acts, but might still have unrealized potentials.

right.label: Unmovable (purely actual)
right.desc: An actualizer with no potentiality at all, and so incapable of being actualized.

distinctions.whyItMatters: Only the second yields the divine attributes. Feser argues the first is incoherent as a first actualizer of existence: any potential in it would need an actualizer, sending us beyond it or into a vicious regress.

illustrations.title: The cooling cup of coffee
illustrations.body:
Hot coffee on your desk has a real potential to become cold — along with potentials to stain the rug or wake you up — but no potential to become chicken soup or a live chicken. When it cools, that potential is actualized, not by itself (a mere potential can’t do anything) but by the actual coolness of the air or by ice cubes you drop in.

Use it to teach three things at once: change is real, potentiality is something rather than nothing (answering Parmenides), and potentials need actual actualizers (the principle of causality).

illustrations.title: The cup on the desk on the floor on the earth — and the hanging lamp
illustrations.body:
The cup is three feet up because the desk holds it *right now*; the desk holds it only because the floor holds the desk *right now*; and so on to the foundation and the earth. A lamp hangs from a chain, held by a fixture, held by the ceiling, held by walls and foundation. Knock out any lower member and everything above it falls at once.

This is Feser’s model of a **hierarchical** series: every intermediate member is like an instrument with borrowed power. Contrast the air conditioner, which keeps cooling the room after you’ve left the house (a **linear** series).

illustrations.title: The painter, the brush — and the infinitely long handle
illustrations.body:
The painter paints the picture; the brush is merely his instrument. A brush has no power to move itself, and it wouldn’t gain any if its handle were infinitely long. If the brush is moving, something with built-in power to move it must be at work.

This shows why ‘first cause’ doesn’t mean ‘earliest cause’, and why making a hierarchical series infinite doesn’t remove the need for a primary cause: more instruments are still just instruments.

illustrations.title: What keeps the water in the coffee existing?
illustrations.body:
The matter that is now water could exist instead as separate hydrogen and oxygen. What actualizes its potential to be water *at this instant*? ‘A reaction in the past’ tells you how it got here; ‘nothing has split it yet’ tells you how it might stop existing. Chemical bonding just restates the question, and atomic structure pushes it one level down to subatomic particles.

We have a hierarchical series of actualizers of *existence*, which must end in something whose existence needs no actualizing — pure actuality.

illustrations.title: The $20 gift
illustrations.body:
I can give you $20 only if I somehow have it: a twenty in my wallet (formally), money in my bank account (virtually), or even the power to print twenty-dollar bills (eminently). If I have it in none of these ways, I can’t give it.

This illustrates the principle of proportionate causality, which Stage 2 uses to show that the cause of all things must contain their forms — not by *being* a cat or a tree, but eminently, as ideas in an intellect.

illustrations.title: Metal detectors, easy courses, and the drunk under the streetlamp
illustrations.body:
A metal detector’s success doesn’t show there’s no wood or stone in the ground. A student who takes only classes he knows he’ll ace can’t conclude other subjects contain nothing important. A drunk who finds things under the streetlamp can’t infer his keys aren’t somewhere in the dark.

Physics deliberately attends only to what can be mathematized, so its silence about causes, potentials, or intrinsic natures is no evidence against them. Feser uses these analogies against Russell, and again against the inertia and quantum objections.

illustrations.title: The black-and-white drawing and the ‘color hold’
illustrations.body:
A line drawing has no color, but that doesn’t show the scene was colorless — the method just can’t record color. In a ‘color hold’, some contours are left out of the ink and supplied only by the color added later; a sharp viewer can still infer, from the lines that are drawn, where the missing edges of a cube must be.

Physics is the line art; physics plus metaphysics is the finished colored picture. Quantum theory, with what Heisenberg compared to Aristotle’s *potentia*, may be line art whose lines hint at the causality they don’t depict.

illustrations.title: Mirrors all the way down
illustrations.body:
A mirror shows the image of a face that is in another mirror, which shows the image in another, and so on without end. Even if such an infinite hall of mirrors were possible, the image must come from an actual face that isn’t just reflecting something else. You can’t have mirror images with no face.

In the same way, an infinite hierarchy of instrumental causes would still need a source of underived causal power outside the series.

illustrations.title: The movie on the screen
illustrations.body:
The image on a cinema screen exists only as long as the projector is running and its bulb is shining. It doesn’t matter how long the film has been playing or whether it had a ‘first frame’; at every instant, the picture exists only because light is being cast on it *now*. Switch off the bulb and the picture doesn’t fade out over centuries — it vanishes instantly.

This is a good way to convey a per se series of existence: the question is not ‘what started the movie?’ but ‘what is keeping the picture there right now?’ (Where the analogy breaks down: the bulb itself needs power; only something purely actual would be a source that needs no source.)

illustrations.title: A train of boxcars with no engine
illustrations.body:
Each boxcar is pulled by the one in front of it. Add more boxcars — a thousand, a million, infinitely many — and you still have no motion at all unless there is an engine, something that pulls without being pulled. Length doesn’t turn borrowed motion into motion that nobody supplies.

This helps skeptics see why ‘just make the regress infinite’ doesn’t work for instrumental causes. Stress that the engine is ‘first’ by *nature* (it pulls on its own power), not merely by position at the front.

misconceptions.myth: The argument claims the universe had a beginning and God started it.
misconceptions.correction: Feser explicitly grants, for argument’s sake, that the universe or a multiverse might have no beginning. The argument concerns what keeps things in existence here and now, at every moment. The Big Bang is irrelevant to it.

misconceptions.myth: The argument rests on the premise that everything has a cause.
misconceptions.correction: Its principle is that whatever goes from potential to actual needs an actualizer. What is purely actual has no potential, so it neither needs nor could have a cause. ‘What caused God?’ attacks a straw man.

misconceptions.myth: ‘First cause’ means the cause that came first in time.
misconceptions.correction: In a hierarchical series, ‘first’ means having underived, built-in causal power, as opposed to the borrowed, instrumental power of the other members. It is first in the order of dependence, not in chronology.

misconceptions.myth: The argument commits the fallacy of composition by inferring that the universe as a whole needs a cause.
misconceptions.correction: No premise is about the universe as a whole. It starts from any single object — a stone, a cup of coffee — existing now. That the conclusion applies to everything is a consequence, not a premise.

misconceptions.myth: If the regress of causes were infinite, there would be no need for a first cause.
misconceptions.correction: True of linear series, but not hierarchical ones. An infinite series of instruments is as powerless as one instrument (an infinitely long brush handle, mirrors with no face). The need for a primary cause has nothing to do with the series being finite.

misconceptions.myth: The argument depends on Aristotle’s outdated physics.
misconceptions.correction: It depends on the metaphysical analysis of change as actualization of potential, not on geocentrism, the four elements or natural places. Science itself presupposes change (observation involves one experience following another), so no scientific theory can refute it.

misconceptions.myth: Because quantum events are indeterministic, they are uncaused.
misconceptions.correction: Causation doesn’t require determinism, only intelligibility. Lead-210 decays according to its nature (formal cause), was generated by something (efficient cause), and is kept in existence by something now. Scientists even call decay the ‘production’ of mercury-206.

misconceptions.myth: Even if there is an Unmoved Mover, it’s just an impersonal force, not God.
misconceptions.correction: Stage 2 argues that a purely actual cause must be one, immutable, eternal, immaterial, perfect, fully good, omnipotent and — via proportionate causality — intelligent and omniscient. The argument goes far beyond a bare ‘first cause’.

misconceptions.myth: A cause must change in order to cause anything, so a purely actual cause is impossible.
misconceptions.correction: That generalizes from the limited causes we observe — a fallacy of accident, like concluding no one over seven feet tall could be president. Our causes change as they act because they are limited (an arm is here and only potentially there). Pure act has no such limits, and the idea isn’t self-contradictory.

misconceptions.myth: The hierarchical series depends on causes being perfectly simultaneous, which physics and relativity rule out.
misconceptions.correction: What makes a series hierarchical is derivative, instrumental power, not simultaneity. Anyway, ‘simultaneous’ need not mean ‘instantaneous’: immediate causes are parts of the same event as their effects, at the same place, so relativity of simultaneity for distant events doesn’t apply.
